paragraphs: Ireland has a new plan to help nature. It is called the draft nature restoration plan. It wants to bring back wild places that have been damaged.
All EU countries must make a plan like this. An EU law from 2024 says so. Ireland sent its plan to the European Commission in September.
The plan has many ideas. It wants more bees by 2030. It wants to fix about 300 kilometres of rivers by 2050. People changed these rivers in the past.
Ireland will also plant about 30 million new trees by 2050. Next year, there will be 20 million euro for small test projects.
Christopher O'Sullivan is the minister for nature. He says farmers, fishers and local groups all helped with the plan. Nature groups say farmers need money every year to do this work.

paragraphs: The Government has published a draft plan to repair damaged nature in Ireland. The plan wants to stop the loss of wildlife and bring back habitats such as wetlands and bogs.

The plan is needed because of a European Union law. The EU Nature Restoration Law was agreed in 2024, and every member country must follow it. Across the EU, countries must restore at least 20% of land and sea areas by 2030, and all damaged nature by 2050.
Ireland sent its draft to the European Commission in September. The Commission will study it and must approve a final version by September next year.

The plan includes several clear goals. A plan for both parts of the island aims to bring back bees by 2030. About 300 kilometres of rivers that were blocked or moved by building work will go back to their natural path by 2050. Ireland will also plant around 30 million extra trees as its share of an EU target of three billion.
By 2050, between 476 and 2,039 square kilometres of land could be restored. The bigger number is larger than County Offaly.

Next year, the Government will give €20 million to a fund for test projects. Christopher O'Sullivan, the Minister of State for nature, said these small projects could later be copied in other places. He called the draft an important step and thanked farmers, foresters, fishers, councils and nature groups for working together.
Groups such as BirdWatch Ireland say farmers and landowners need money for many years, not just one, to do this work properly.

歐盟《自然復育法》於 2024 年通過，每個成員國都必須遵守。
在整個歐盟，各國必須在 2030 年前恢復至少 20% 的陸地與海洋區域，並在 2050 年前恢復所有受損的自然環境。
愛爾蘭在九月把草案送交歐盟執委會。
執委會將研究草案，並必須在明年九月前核准最終版本。

大約 300 公里因工程而被阻斷或改道的河流，將在 2050 年前恢復自然河道。

明年政府將撥出兩千萬歐元成立試驗計畫基金。
負責自然事務的國務部長克里斯多福·歐蘇利文說，這些小型計畫日後可以在其他地方複製。

paragraphs: The Government has published a draft nature restoration plan that aims to reverse the steep decline in Ireland's biodiversity and repair damaged habitats such as wetlands and peatlands.

The plan is a legal requirement. The EU Nature Restoration Regulation, adopted in 2024, is binding on every member state. It sets a target of restoring at least 20% of the EU's land and sea by 2030 and all degraded ecosystems by 2050.
Ireland submitted its draft to the European Commission in September, and the Commission will review it before the deadline for approval in September 2027.

Among its key measures is a cross-border pollinator plan to restore bee populations by 2030. Around 300 kilometres of rivers that were blocked or diverted by engineering works are to be returned to their original course by 2050. Ireland's share of the EU's pledge to plant three billion additional trees works out at roughly 30 million.
In total, between 476 and 2,039 square kilometres of the State could be restored by 2050, and the upper figure is larger than County Offaly.

A €20 million pathfinder fund will be available next year for pilot projects. Christopher O'Sullivan, Minister of State for Nature, Heritage and Biodiversity, described the draft as an important milestone and praised the collaboration between farming, forestry, fishing, local authorities and environmental groups. He said the pilots could be scaled up elsewhere.

However, environmental organisations, including BirdWatch Ireland and the Climate Change Advisory Council, insist that only multi-annual funding will allow farmers and landowners to restore habitats properly.

paragraphs: The Government has unveiled a draft nature restoration plan intended to halt and ultimately reverse the precipitous decline in Ireland's biodiversity, with wetlands and peatlands among the habitats earmarked for repair.

The initiative is far from voluntary. Under the EU Nature Restoration Regulation, adopted in 2024, every member state is obliged to act, and the bloc as a whole must rehabilitate at least a fifth of its land and sea by 2030 and every degraded ecosystem by 2050.
Ireland lodged its draft with the European Commission in September, and Brussels will scrutinise it ahead of a September 2027 deadline for sign-off.

The headline commitments are ambitious. A cross-border pollinator strategy seeks to revive dwindling bee numbers by 2030, while some 300 kilometres of rivers that were straightened, dammed or diverted by engineering works are to be coaxed back to their original channels by 2050. Ireland's proportional contribution to the EU's pledge of three billion additional trees amounts to roughly 30 million.
All told, somewhere between 476 and 2,039 square kilometres could be restored by mid-century, the upper estimate eclipsing the entire area of County Offaly.

A €20 million pathfinder fund will be rolled out next year to bankroll pilot schemes. Christopher O'Sullivan, the Minister of State with responsibility for nature, hailed the draft as a milestone forged through genuine collaboration between farmers, foresters, fishers, councils and conservationists, and expressed hope that successful pilots would be replicated nationwide.

Nonetheless, conservation bodies such as BirdWatch Ireland and the Climate Change Advisory Council caution that, without dependable multi-annual funding, landowners will have little incentive to undertake meaningful restoration.

paragraphs: The Irish Government has published a draft nature restoration plan, the principal objective of which is to arrest and subsequently reverse the substantial decline in national biodiversity, with particular emphasis on wetlands and peatlands.

Crucially, the plan is a statutory obligation rather than a discretionary policy. The EU Nature Restoration Regulation, adopted in 2024, is legally binding on all member states and stipulates that at least 20% of the Union's land and marine area must be restored by 2030, and all degraded ecosystems by 2050.
Ireland submitted its draft to the European Commission in September; consequently, the Commission will evaluate the proposal prior to the approval deadline of September 2027.

The plan comprises a number of quantifiable targets. A cross-border pollinator strategy aims to restore bee populations by 2030, whereas approximately 300 kilometres of rivers altered by engineering works are to be returned to their original course by 2050. Furthermore, Ireland's proportional share of the EU commitment to plant three billion additional trees equates to roughly 30 million.
Overall, the area designated for restoration by 2050 ranges from 476 to 2,039 square kilometres, the latter exceeding the total area of County Offaly.

In terms of financing, a €20 million pathfinder fund will be allocated next year to support pilot projects. Christopher O'Sullivan, Minister of State for Nature, Heritage and Biodiversity, characterised the draft as a significant milestone and attributed its development to extensive collaboration among agricultural, forestry, fishing, local government and environmental stakeholders. He further suggested that effective pilots could be replicated on a larger scale.

Nevertheless, organisations including BirdWatch Ireland and the Climate Change Advisory Council maintain that the success of the plan is contingent upon multi-annual funding, without which landowners are unlikely to restore habitats effectively.

關鍵在於，這個計畫是法定義務，而非可自行決定的政策。
2024 年通過的歐盟《自然復育條例》對所有成員國具有法律約束力，並規定歐盟至少 20% 的陸地與海域必須在 2030 年前恢復，所有退化的生態系統則須在 2050 年前恢復。
